name: AT SCHOOL: SPEAKING UP
safetyNote: Most things at school feel like a big deal and turn out not to be. Safety is the exception. If you are worried that somebody could get hurt, tell an adult. Do not wait until you are sure. Being asked about something you did is the other kind of moment. That is when you slow down and ask for a parent first.

questions.q: You send a tip to OK2SAY, Michigan's school safety line. What happens to it first?

options.text: It goes to a trained person at the state police, who decides where to send it.
It goes straight to your principal with your name attached.
options.explanation: Tips reach the state police first, and your name is not attached when they pass one on.

options.text: It sits there until you confirm who you are.
options.explanation: You never have to give a name. You do leave a phone number or email so they can ask you questions.

options.text: It comes back to you with an answer about what they will do.
options.explanation: You get a note saying it arrived. What happens after that is not something you get told.

questions.hint: Who reads it before the school does?
questions.principle: OK2SAY is Michigan's student safety tip line. The state police run it, and anybody can use it, day or night. A trained person reads what you send, asks you questions if they need more, and decides who should get it. That might be your school, local police, or a mental health agency. Life threats and crimes happening now go to police first. Everything else usually reaches a school administrator the next school day.

keyPhrase.quote: A person reads it, not a machine.
keyPhrase.gloss: Trained state police staff sort every tip.

scenario.setup: Your kitchen table, late. The app is open on your phone.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Are you actually going to send that?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I think so. I don't even know who reads these.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Some office somewhere.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: State police, apparently. I'm sending it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: It gets read tonight by somebody whose job is reading them.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The thing you know stays with only you, and nobody else can act on it.

scenario.note: If somebody is in danger right now, that is a 911 call, not a tip.

questions.q: You want to send an OK2SAY tip but you are scared it gets back to you. What happens to your name?

options.text: It stays sealed unless you agree to release it or a judge orders it out.
It goes on the report, so anybody at school can ask for it.
options.explanation: Your name is not passed along with the tip. The protection is a state law, not a school practice.

options.text: It stays sealed no matter what, with no exception.
options.explanation: There is one exception, and it is for tips somebody sent falsely to cause trouble.

options.text: It depends on your district, since each one writes its own rule.
options.explanation: This one is not up to a district. The same state law covers every school in Michigan.

questions.hint: Who has to agree before anybody learns it was you?
questions.principle: The Student Safety Act protects who you are. Your name can be released only if you say yes. If you are under 18, a parent can say yes too. A judge can also order it. It is kept out of public records requests. The tip line cannot even hand over the address a tip came from without a court order. You never have to give your name. You do leave a phone number or email, so a technician can ask you more.

keyPhrase.quote: They can't hand my name over without a judge.
keyPhrase.gloss: It is a law, not a promise.

scenario.setup: The bus stop after school. Your friend is scrolling.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: If you send that, everybody will know it was you.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: They can't hand my name over without a judge.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Says who?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: It's a state law. I looked it up.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You send it knowing what is actually protecting you.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The thing that stops you is a rumor about how it works.

scenario.note: The protection covers your name. It does not stop people guessing, so keep it to yourself.

questions.q: You heard something that worries you about a classmate, but you are not certain it is real. What should you do?

options.text: Report what you heard, and say plainly which part you are unsure about.
Wait until you know for sure, so you do not waste anybody's time.
options.explanation: Nobody expects you to be sure. Waiting for certainty is how things get missed.

options.text: Ask around first to find out whether it is even true.
options.explanation: Asking around warns people and spreads something that may not be true. It is the one move that makes it worse.

options.text: Say nothing. Being wrong about it would be worse than staying quiet.
options.explanation: Being wrong costs you very little here. Being right and silent is the expensive one.

questions.hint: Who is supposed to be doing the checking, you or them?
questions.principle: You are not the investigator. Nobody expects you to be sure. The people who take tips are trained to ask questions, and they would rather hear something that turns out to be nothing than miss something real. Saying which part you are unsure about is useful, not weak, because it tells them what to check. Asking around first is the one thing that makes it worse. It warns people, and it spreads something that might not be true.

keyPhrase.quote: I'm not sure about this part, but here is what I heard.
keyPhrase.gloss: Not being sure is a reason to say more, not less.

scenario.setup: The cafeteria. You are half listening to the next table.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: You didn't actually hear it, though.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I heard enough that I don't want to be wrong about it.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Ask him first.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: No. I'll say what I heard and let them sort it out.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Somebody trained gets to decide what it is worth, which was never your job.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Everybody involved finds out you were asking, and nothing gets checked.

scenario.note: Do not investigate. Repeating what you heard to the wrong person is its own problem.

questions.q: Somebody has a weapon at school right now. Which one do you use?

options.text: Call 911, because right now is the one thing a tip line is not for.
Send a tip, since that is exactly what the tip line is there for.
options.explanation: A tip still has to be read and passed along. That is time you do not have when it is happening now.

options.text: Tell a teacher after class, so you do not make a scene.
options.explanation: After class is too late for this one. The quiet option is the wrong option here.

options.text: Post it, since that reaches more people faster than anything else.
options.explanation: A post reaches people who cannot do anything and warns the one person who can move.

questions.hint: How fast is this moving, and how fast is each way of telling?
questions.principle: OK2SAY, Michigan's school safety tip line, is an early warning system, not an emergency line. It runs day and night, but a technician still has to read your message and pass it on. That is time you do not have when something is happening right now. For right now, call 911. OK2SAY says the same thing itself. Tips about a plan, a pattern, or something that worries you are exactly what it is for.

keyPhrase.quote: Right now means 911. Later means the tip line.
keyPhrase.gloss: Match the way you tell it to how fast it is moving.

scenario.setup: The hallway before third hour. Somebody tells you what they just saw.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: He's got something in his bag. I saw it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Is he here right now?

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: He's in the building.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Then I'm calling 911, not typing a tip.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: People who can move in minutes find out in minutes.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The fastest thing you had gets used on the slowest way to tell it.

scenario.note: Get somewhere safe first. Make the call from there, not from the hallway.

questions.q: You are about to report that a classmate brought a weapon to school. Your friend calls that snitching. What is the honest answer?

options.text: It might feel like that, and this one is serious enough to do it anyway.
It is snitching, so stay out of it and let somebody else deal with it.
options.explanation: Snitching is giving somebody up to get them in trouble. This is about somebody getting hurt.

options.text: Telling an adult about anything a classmate does is always right.
options.explanation: Reporting somebody for skipping class is a different thing, and that one is tattling.

options.text: It does not matter, since nobody will ever find out it was you.
options.explanation: People sometimes guess. The reason to do it is that it matters, not that it is untraceable.

questions.hint: Trouble for them, or safety for somebody?
questions.principle: The feeling is real and worth naming. Telling can make you the person who told, and that is a cost. So the line matters. Safety is the line: somebody getting hurt, a weapon, a threat, a person in real trouble. Skipping class or being mean to you is not that, and reporting those is tattling. When it is a safety thing, the risk of staying quiet is bigger than the risk of being called a name for a week.

keyPhrase.quote: This one is too serious to worry about the word.
keyPhrase.gloss: Safety is the line. Annoying is not.

scenario.setup: The locker room after practice. Two of you are still there.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: You're not going to say anything, right?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: This one I am.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: That's snitching.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Maybe it looks like it. Somebody could get hurt, so I don't care.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You take the cost with your eyes open instead of pretending it is not there.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: A word decides it, and the word was never about this kind of thing.

scenario.note: You do not have to win the argument. You can end it and still send the tip.

questions.q: A week ago somebody told you a plan to hurt another student, and you said nothing. Is it too late now?

options.text: No. Reporting late is still reporting, and waiting longer does not help you.
Yes. Knowing about it for a week makes you part of it now.
options.explanation: Knowing something is not the same as being part of it. The week does not turn you into a participant.

options.text: Yes. Waiting that long is going to look like you were in on it.
options.explanation: How it looks is not the test, and it looks worse in a week than it does today.

options.text: No, but you should explain your whole week before you get to the point.
options.explanation: The report is about what you know, not about you. Explaining yourself first buries the part that matters.

questions.hint: What does one more week change?
questions.principle: Waiting does not put you in trouble, and the fear that it does keeps people quiet forever. Knowing something is not the same as being part of it. What the week changes is the odds that the thing you know about actually happens. If you are worried how the delay looks, you can say when you heard it and why you sat on it. That is one sentence. It does not change what the report is about.

keyPhrase.quote: I heard it a week ago. I should have said it then.
keyPhrase.gloss: Late is not too late.

scenario.setup: Your kitchen table. You have had your phone in your hand for an hour.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: You've been quiet all night.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I've known about something for a week.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Since when do you sit on things?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Since I worked out I'd have to explain the week.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The week is a sentence in the report instead of the reason there is no report.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It turns into two weeks, and then into never.

scenario.note: Telling a parent counts. It does not all have to go through a form.

questions.q: Three days after your OK2SAY tip, you have heard nothing back. What can you tell from that?

options.text: Nothing at all. Nobody is allowed to tell you how it turned out.
It probably got lost, since a real report comes back with an answer.
options.explanation: No update is the normal ending. The tip line does not report back to the person who sent one.

options.text: Nothing was done, since nothing at school looks any different.
options.explanation: Most of what happens is a conversation you would never see. Quiet is not the same as nothing.

options.text: Your name was needed after all before anybody could act.
options.explanation: A tip works without your name. What you leave is a way to be asked questions, not an identity.

questions.hint: Is there anybody who can tell you?
questions.principle: Silence afterward is normal. It does not mean nothing happened. The tip line does not send you an update. Schools do write up what they did, and that write up is private. A federal law also stops a school from telling you what happened to another student. It is the same law that stops them telling anybody about you. So the quiet is the way it was built.

keyPhrase.quote: No news is not the same as nothing happened.
keyPhrase.gloss: You are not going to be told, and that is deliberately.

scenario.setup: The classroom before the bell. Everything looks completely normal.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Guess nothing came of it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: We wouldn't know either way.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Somebody would have said something.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: They're not allowed to. That part is private.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You stop reading the silence as an answer, because it is not one.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You decide it did not work, and next time you do not bother.

scenario.note: Not hearing back is the design, not a failure. Send the next one anyway.

questions.q: Somebody suggests sending a fake tip about a person they are angry at. Where does that go?

options.text: Into a police matter, since a prosecutor can ask a judge to unseal it.
Nowhere. It is a prank, and pranks are not a real thing.
options.explanation: Filing a false report to mislead police can be treated as a crime. That is not a prank.

options.text: It disappears, because the line is confidential whatever the tip says.
options.explanation: False tips are the one written exception to that confidentiality. A judge can open one up.

options.text: Into school discipline only, since the whole thing is a school matter.
options.explanation: It can be a school matter and a police matter at once. Neither one waits for the other.

questions.hint: There is one door in the wall. What is it for?
questions.principle: The privacy rule has one hole in it, and this is the hole. A prosecutor who thinks a tip was sent falsely can ask a court to open it up. That includes anything that shows who sent it. A judge decides. Filing a false report to mislead police can be treated as a crime. So a fake tip is not a joke that vanishes into a phone. It is the one case the law was written to reach.

keyPhrase.quote: The one kind they can open up is a fake one.
keyPhrase.gloss: False reports are the exception to the whole rule.

scenario.setup: The gym doorway before practice. Somebody is holding out a phone.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Just send one about him. Nobody can tell.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: That's the one kind they can trace.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: You're making that up.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: A judge can open up a fake one. I'm not doing it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Nothing happens, which is the correct amount of things to happen.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: A phone with your number on it sent a report a prosecutor can open.

scenario.note: Sending it from somebody else's phone does not help either of you.

questions.q: You told a teacher that a classmate keeps threatening another student. A week later nothing has changed. What now?

options.text: Tell somebody higher up, and tell a parent. One adult is not the whole school.
Send a tip so the state can make the school act on it.
options.explanation: A tip line passes information along. It cannot overturn what a school decided to do.

options.text: Nothing more. You told somebody, so it belongs to them now.
options.explanation: Telling one adult is a start, not the whole job. If nothing moved, somebody else needs to hear it.

options.text: Wait it out, since somebody will get to it eventually.
options.explanation: Waiting works when something is already moving. Nothing here says anything is.

questions.hint: Is one teacher the same thing as the school?
questions.principle: Telling one adult is the start. Sometimes it is enough and sometimes the message stops there. If nothing has moved, go up: a counselor, an assistant principal, the principal, the district office. Tell a parent too, because a parent can ask questions a student cannot. A tip line is useful here as another way in, but it cannot force a school to reach a different answer. That part is escalation, not reporting.

keyPhrase.quote: I already told somebody, and nothing happened.
keyPhrase.gloss: One adult is a start, not the whole school.

scenario.setup: The hallway outside the counselor's room at school.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I told Mr. K last week and nothing happened.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Did you tell anybody else?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: No. I thought that was it.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It usually isn't.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: A second adult knows, and that one can go further than the first.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It stops with one person who may have already forgotten it.

scenario.note: Going over somebody's head is allowed. Say what you already told and who you told.

questions.q: Something happened at the bus stop, not on school grounds. Is that still OK2SAY's business?

options.text: Yes. The bus stop is on the list, along with the bus and the walk to school.
No. It has to happen on school property to count.
options.explanation: The list is wider than the building. School events, the bus, the bus stop, and the walk are all on it.

options.text: No, unless it happened during the school day.
options.explanation: The line runs all day, all night, and through the summer. School hours are not the test.

options.text: Yes, but only if your own district runs that particular stop.
options.explanation: It covers every public and private school in Michigan. Whose stop it is does not decide it.

questions.hint: The line follows something. Is it the building?
questions.principle: OK2SAY covers more ground than most people think. Michigan takes reports about anything on school property. It also covers a school event, the school bus, the bus stop, and the way to and from school. It covers every public and private school in the state, from kindergarten to twelfth grade. It runs day and night, and all summer, because the things worth reporting do not keep school hours.

keyPhrase.quote: The bus stop counts. So does the walk.
keyPhrase.gloss: It follows the school day, not the building.

scenario.setup: The bus stop after school, ten minutes after the bus pulls away.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: It wasn't on school property, so who cares.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: It's still on the list.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Since when?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Bus, bus stop, the walk. All of it counts.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The thing that happened gets reported to people who can act on it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: A line on a map decides it, and the line is in the wrong place.

scenario.note: If it is happening at the stop right now, that is a 911 call like anywhere else.

questions.q: A teacher says the armband you are wearing for a cause is not allowed. What is the actual test?

options.text: Whether it would really disrupt school, not whether an adult dislikes it.
Whether the school agrees with what it says.
options.explanation: Agreement is not the test. A school cannot ban a message just because it does not like the message.

options.text: Whether anybody was bothered by seeing it.
options.explanation: Somebody being annoyed is not a disruption. The bar is real interference with school.

options.text: Nothing at all. A school cannot limit what you wear.
options.explanation: Schools can act when speech would really disrupt school or trample somebody else's rights.

questions.hint: Two different things could be true: they hate it, and it changes nothing.
questions.principle: Students do not lose free speech at the school door. The Supreme Court said so in 1969, in a case about students who wore black armbands to protest a war, and the rule from that case is still the test. A school can step in when speech would really disrupt school or trample somebody else's rights. Not liking the message is not enough. Somebody being annoyed is not enough either. In 2003 a Dearborn student was told to turn a political t-shirt inside out or go home. He went home, and a judge ordered the school to let him wear it.

keyPhrase.quote: Being disliked is not the same as being disruptive.
keyPhrase.gloss: The test is real disruption, not how adults feel.

scenario.setup: First hour. A teacher stops at your desk and points at your sleeve.

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: That's going to have to come off.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Has it caused a problem?

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: It might.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'll ask the office which rule it breaks.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The question gets asked where somebody has to answer it in writing.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It comes off, and nobody ever names the rule.

scenario.note: Take it off if you are told to. Ask which rule afterward, not in front of the class.

questions.q: You give a speech at a school assembly and fill it with crude jokes. Can the school do anything?

options.text: Yes. Lewd talk at a school event is one of the clear exceptions.
No. Crude is not the same as disruptive, so it is covered.
options.explanation: Lewd speech at a school event is its own exception. It does not have to disrupt anything.

options.text: No, unless the school warned you about that in advance.
options.explanation: This one does not depend on a handbook. It is a rule from the Supreme Court, not the district.

options.text: Yes, but only if somebody actually complained about it.
options.explanation: Nobody has to complain. The school's own event is the school's own audience.

questions.hint: Whose stage were you standing on?
questions.principle: Two exceptions here are settled. A school can act on crude or lewd talk at a school event. The Supreme Court decided that in 1986, after a student gave a speech full of crude jokes at an assembly. A school can also act on speech at a school event that pushes illegal drug use. That was decided in 2007. Both are narrower than they sound. They are about the school's own events, not about everything you ever say.

keyPhrase.quote: A school event is the school's own audience.
keyPhrase.gloss: Crude at an assembly is its own exception.

scenario.setup: The school assembly, right after you sit back down.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: We need to talk about that speech.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: People laughed.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: That isn't the standard.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. What is the rule, so I know for next time?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You find out where the line actually is instead of guessing at it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You argue the wrong point and never learn the right one.

scenario.note: This is not the moment to test it. Ask what the rule is when nobody is watching.

questions.q: The principal cuts your article from the school paper. What makes that different from your own post?

options.text: The paper carries the school's name and your own post does not.
Nothing at all, since your writing is your writing either way.
options.explanation: Whose name is on the publication changes the rule. School-sponsored work follows school rules.

options.text: The format, since a newspaper gets more protection than a post.
options.explanation: It runs the other way here. A school paper carries the school's name and your own post does not.

options.text: The topic, since a school can only cut something that is untrue.
options.explanation: True and false is not the test. School-sponsored work can be cut for reasons tied to teaching.

questions.hint: Whose name is printed at the top of the page?
questions.principle: Work the school puts its name on is treated differently. In 1988 the Supreme Court let a principal pull pages from a student newspaper. The paper was part of a class and it carried the school's name. Schools can control school-sponsored work for reasons tied to teaching. That is a real limit on the paper. It says nothing about what you write on your own time, which is a different question with a different answer.

keyPhrase.quote: Whose name is on it changes the rule.
keyPhrase.gloss: School-sponsored work follows school rules.

scenario.setup: The journalism room after school. The layout is up on the screen.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: This one isn't running.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can you tell me why?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It's the school's paper.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Then can I run it somewhere that isn't?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The piece exists somewhere, and the rule got named out loud.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It comes out of the layout and that is the end of it.

scenario.note: Arguing in the room rarely changes the layout. Ask where else it could run.

questions.q: You post something on a Saturday, from home, about a teacher. How far does the school's reach go?

options.text: Not very far. Off campus and on your own time is mostly outside it.
All the way. You are a student everywhere, all of the time.
options.explanation: Being a student does not follow you into every hour of your life. Off campus, the school's reason to act is much weaker.

options.text: Nowhere at all. Off campus, a school is just another adult.
options.explanation: Less reach is not no reach. Threats, harassment aimed at somebody, and cheating still get in.

options.text: As far as it wants, unless you take the post down first.
options.explanation: Taking it down does not unsend it. Screenshots are why that plan almost never works.

questions.hint: Two things are true at once, and neither one is all or nothing.
questions.principle: In 2021 the Supreme Court ruled for a student who posted an angry message on a weekend, away from school, after she did not make a team. The Court said schools have much less reason to police speech that happens off campus and outside school hours. Less is not none. Threats, harassment aimed at a person, and cheating still reach into school. But the ordinary rule is that your own time is your own.

keyPhrase.quote: Off campus and off hours is mostly not theirs.
keyPhrase.gloss: Less reach is not no reach.

scenario.setup: Your kitchen on Saturday. The post is up and the phone will not stop.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Take it down.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: It's Saturday and I'm not at school.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Take it down anyway.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. I still want to know which rule they'd use.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You find out what they are actually claiming before you agree it applies.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You assume they can do anything, and act like it.

scenario.note: Threats and harassment are the exceptions. Off campus does not cover those.

questions.q: A staff member says she can read your messages because you sent them on the school Chromebook. What is true?

options.text: A school laptop and a school account belong to the school, so mostly she can.
She would need the same reason she needs to read your own phone.
options.explanation: Your phone is yours and the Chromebook is not. They are not the same question.

options.text: The same rule would cover your own phone on the school wifi.
options.explanation: Using their wifi does not hand them your phone. The device is what changes it.

options.text: She has to warn you first before she reads anything you wrote.
options.explanation: There is no warning rule. The handbook usually says it once, at the start of the year.

questions.hint: Whose machine did you type it on?
questions.principle: A school Chromebook and a school email account belong to the school, the same way a locker does. Districts usually spell this out in the handbook: no privacy on district devices or district accounts. Your own phone is a different question and stays yours. The practical version is short. If you would not want it read, do not type it on their machine or send it from their account. It is not a hidden rule. It is a question of whose equipment it is.

keyPhrase.quote: Their laptop, their account, their rules.
keyPhrase.gloss: Your own phone is a different question.

scenario.setup: The computer lab. Your school account is open on the screen.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: I can see everything that goes through that account.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Is that in the handbook?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It is.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Then I'll keep the rest on my own phone.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You learn where the line is while nothing is happening, which is the cheap time to learn it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You find out what was readable after somebody has read it.

scenario.note: Assume anything on a school device can be read. That is the safe default, not a punishment.

questions.q: An assistant principal tells you to delete a post you made at home. What is worth doing before it is gone?

options.text: Screenshot it, so there is a copy of what it actually said.
Nothing. Once it is deleted the whole thing is over.
options.explanation: Other people already have copies. Deleting takes away yours and leaves theirs alone.

options.text: Post an explanation, so everybody knows your side of it.
options.explanation: A second post is a second thing to answer for. It does not settle the first one.

options.text: Not much, since a post from home was never theirs to ask about.
options.explanation: Mostly it is not theirs, and there are exceptions. Either way the copy is what you will want later.

questions.hint: What disappears along with the post?
questions.principle: What you post from home, on your own time, is mostly outside what a school can act on. Mostly is not always, and that is a question for later. What matters right now is that deleting it does not undo it. Other people have screenshots and you will not. So take your own copy first. Then take it down if you are told to, ask which rule they say it breaks, and tell a parent that night.

keyPhrase.quote: I want a copy of it before it comes down.
keyPhrase.gloss: Deleting removes your copy, not theirs.

scenario.setup: The school office, second hour. A laptop is turned toward you.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: I need that taken down today.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can I screenshot it first?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Why would you need that?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: So there's a copy of what it actually said.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: What was really posted still exists, and it is not only in somebody's memory.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It is gone, and the only description left is whoever describes it next.

scenario.note: Take it down if you are told to. The copy is the part worth asking about.

questions.q: You leave class for a protest walkout. What can the school do about it?

options.text: Treat it as an unexcused absence, the same as any other class you missed.
Nothing, since a protest is protected speech.
options.explanation: The speech is protected. Being in class is a separate rule, and leaving it is still leaving it.

options.text: Punish it harder than a normal skip, because of what you were protesting.
options.explanation: The message is the one thing they cannot add punishment for. The absence is the part they can act on.

options.text: Cancel the absence, since a protest is not the same as skipping.
options.explanation: It counts as a missed class. The reason for missing it does not erase the missing.

questions.hint: Two separate things happened. Which one is the school's?
questions.principle: A walkout is two things at once. One is speech, and the school does not get to punish you for what you were walking out about. The other is that you were not in class, and that is an ordinary absence with ordinary consequences. So expect what any skipped class gets, and no more. If the punishment is heavier than the usual one, the difference is the part worth asking about, in writing, with a parent.

keyPhrase.quote: Missing class is the part they can act on.
keyPhrase.gloss: The absence counts. The message does not.

scenario.setup: The school steps during fourth hour, with sixty other students.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Everybody out here is getting marked absent.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Same as any other absence?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Same as any other.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. That's what I expected.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know what you are paying for it, and you can check that the price does not change.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Anything they add on top of the absence goes unnoticed and unasked about.

scenario.note: Expect the absence. Ask about anything beyond it, afterward, with a parent.

questions.q: A teacher says your shirt is a distraction and has to go. What does distraction have to mean here?

options.text: Real interference with school, not an adult disliking the message.
Whatever a teacher says it means on the day.
options.explanation: Somebody being bothered is not the test. Real interference with school is.

options.text: Anything the dress code lists, and nothing beyond that.
options.explanation: A dress code is real, and it still cannot be used to reach a message the school dislikes.

options.text: The principal's call, since only a principal enforces it.
options.explanation: Any staff member enforces a dress code. Who says it is not what makes it right or wrong.

questions.hint: Is it the shirt, or is it what the shirt says?
questions.principle: Schools can have a dress code, and most of it has nothing to do with speech. The question is what the word distraction is doing. If it means real interference with school, it is the actual test. If it means an adult does not like the message, it is not, and that is the version courts have thrown out. You are not going to settle that in a hallway. Ask which line of the dress code it breaks, write down the answer, and take it home.

keyPhrase.quote: Which part of the dress code is that?
keyPhrase.gloss: Ask for the rule, not the opinion.

scenario.setup: The hallway between second and third hour.

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: That shirt is a distraction. Turn it inside out.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Which part of the dress code is it?

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: We can look it up later.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay, I'll turn it around. I'd still like to know.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Somebody has to find the rule, and now there is a record that you asked.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The word does the work, and nobody ever has to point at a rule.

scenario.note: Turn it inside out if you are told to. The rule question is for the office, not the hallway.

questions.q: Something you said at school got you suspended and also got police involved. What is true about those two?

options.text: They run side by side, on different rules and different clocks.
They run in order, since the school waits for the police part.
options.explanation: Neither waits. School discipline usually moves in days and a case can take months.

options.text: They rise and fall together, so fixing one fixes the other.
options.explanation: A win in one does not clear the other. They are decided separately, by different people.

options.text: They never touch, since words at school cannot reach a police case.
options.explanation: Staff can be asked what you said, and a school report can travel with it.

questions.hint: How many places is this happening in?
questions.principle: One thing you said turned into two problems, and they do not travel together. The school runs its own process on its own rules and it usually moves fast. A police matter runs on different rules and takes much longer. Winning one does not end the other. That matters most for what you say, because an explanation you give to settle the school part can show up in the other one. This is where you ask for a parent even if the school part feels small.

keyPhrase.quote: This is two problems, not one.
keyPhrase.gloss: Two systems, side by side, on different clocks.

scenario.setup: The school office. Somebody from outside the building is waiting.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: We'll handle our side today.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Is somebody else handling another side?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: That's not up to us.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Then I'd rather wait for my mom before I say anything.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You stop at the point where the second system shows up.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: One explanation gets used twice, in two places, on two sets of rules.

scenario.note: Be polite about the school part and quiet about the rest. Those are not the same thing.

questions.q: You think a school rule is wrong and you want it changed. How do you get that process started?

options.text: Ask for the rule in writing, then ask who can change it and when they meet.
Post about it, since enough attention makes them move.
options.explanation: Attention is not a process. The people who can change a rule get reached a different way.

options.text: Argue it out with the teacher who enforces it.
options.explanation: The person enforcing a rule usually cannot change it. That argument goes nowhere by design.

options.text: Nothing. Students do not get a say in school rules.
options.explanation: Students get a say more often than they use it. Board meetings are usually open to anybody.

questions.hint: Who wrote the rule, and who is only enforcing it?
questions.principle: Rules come from somewhere, and it is almost never the person telling you about one. Most school rules live in a district policy that a school board adopted, and board meetings have to be open. Michigan's Open Meetings Act says a person gets to speak at one, under whatever rules the board sets, and there is no age limit in it. So the order is short. Get the rule in writing. Find out who adopted it. Find out when they meet. Bring the rule with you and say what you would change.

keyPhrase.quote: Who can actually change this rule?
keyPhrase.gloss: Take it to whoever wrote it, not whoever said it.

scenario.setup: The school office at lunch, asking for a copy of the policy.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can I get the phone policy in writing?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It's in the handbook.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Who decided it? I want to ask them about it.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: That would be the board.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You end up in front of the people who can actually change it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You spend a year arguing with people who could never have changed it.

scenario.note: Bring the rule and one clear change. Arguing without either one goes nowhere.

questions.q: Before a school suspends you for a few days, what are you owed?

options.text: Being told what you are accused of, and a chance to give your side.
A full hearing with a lawyer before you can be sent home.
options.explanation: A short suspension is not a courtroom. What it takes is notice and a chance to answer.

options.text: Nothing. A school can send you home and explain afterward.
options.explanation: Even a short suspension takes notice and a chance to respond first, in almost every case.

options.text: A written decision first, since nothing counts until it is on paper.
options.explanation: It can be a conversation in an office. Paper is worth asking for, but it is not what makes it real.

questions.hint: It is short, so it is small. Is small the same as nothing?
questions.principle: In 1975 the Supreme Court decided a case about students suspended for up to ten days with no hearing at all. The Court said even a short suspension takes two things. The school has to tell you what you are accused of, and it has to give you a chance to tell your side. That can be a conversation in an office rather than a hearing. If you are a danger to somebody right then, the school can remove you first and do that part as soon as it can afterward.

keyPhrase.quote: What am I accused of, and can I tell my side?
keyPhrase.gloss: Notice and a chance to answer. That is the floor.

scenario.setup: The school office, first thing in the morning.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: You're out for three days.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: What am I accused of?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: You know what this is about.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'd still like to hear it, and I want to tell you my side.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Both of the things you are owed happen, and somebody has to say what the accusation is.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You are out for three days and nobody ever had to name what for.

scenario.note: Ask both questions calmly. This is the one part that is supposed to happen before you leave.

questions.q: The school is talking about a fifteen day suspension. What changes at that length?

options.text: Past ten days, the school has to show it went through the steps.
Nothing changes. Every suspension works about the same way.
options.explanation: They do not. The law puts a heavier requirement on removals longer than ten days.

options.text: The rules only shift at expulsion, so not yet.
options.explanation: The line sits at ten days, well before expulsion. Fifteen days is already past it.

options.text: You get a lawyer and a hearing, since fifteen days is serious.
options.explanation: Longer does not turn it into a court case. What changes is what the school has to show, not who speaks for you.

questions.hint: Count the days. Is that number over a line somewhere?
questions.principle: Michigan draws a line at ten days. For ten days or fewer, the school still has to go through seven set things before it decides. Past ten days, or for an expulsion, the law starts from the idea that it is not justified. The district has to show it went through each of the seven. That is the part worth knowing at fifteen days, because it puts the work on the school and not on you.

keyPhrase.quote: Is this more than ten days?
keyPhrase.gloss: Ten days is where the law gets heavier.

scenario.setup: The school office with a letter on the desk between you.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: The suspension is fifteen days.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: That's more than ten.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It is.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Then can we go through the seven factors?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The number gets noticed out loud, and the number is what changes the rules.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Fifteen and five feel like the same kind of thing, and only one of them is.

scenario.note: The number of days is the first thing to write down. Everything else follows from it.

questions.q: A principal decides to suspend you for three days. What does Michigan require before that?

options.text: Going through a set list of things the law names, every time.
Going through that list only when a parent asks for it.
options.explanation: It is required whether or not anybody brings it up. You do not have to request it.

options.text: Going through none of it. Three days is too short to matter.
options.explanation: The list applies to a three day suspension the same as to an expulsion. Short is not exempt.

options.text: Going through a police report first, so something is on record.
options.explanation: School discipline does not wait for police, and most of it never involves them.

questions.hint: Does a short one get a pass on this?
questions.principle: Michigan law names seven things a school has to weigh before it suspends or expels a student. Your age. Your record. Whether you have a disability. How bad it was. Whether it put anybody at risk. Whether the school will try restorative practices. Whether a smaller step would fix it. All seven are required, and three days counts the same as an expulsion.

keyPhrase.quote: Did you go through the seven factors?
keyPhrase.gloss: Required every time, not only for the long ones.

scenario.setup: The school office. The decision has already been made.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Three days, starting tomorrow.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Did you go through the seven factors?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: That's for the long ones.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I don't think it is. Can my mom ask about that?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The question is on the record even if nobody answers it today.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Nobody ever has to say whether the required part happened.

scenario.note: Ask the question once. Let a parent be the one who follows it up.

questions.q: The school sends you home the same morning, before anybody talks to you about it. When is that allowed?

options.text: When you are a danger right then. The talking has to happen soon after.
Whenever a principal decides that is the easier way to do it.
options.explanation: Easier is not the test. Notice and a chance to answer come first in almost every case.

options.text: Never. Nothing at all can happen before you get to answer.
options.explanation: There is one exception, and it is for right now. Then the answering happens as soon as it can.

options.text: Any time the police are involved in it too.
options.explanation: Police being involved does not remove the school's own steps. The two run on their own rules.

questions.hint: What would make waiting the wrong call?
questions.principle: The ordinary order is that a school tells you what you are accused of and lets you answer before you go home. There is one exception. If you are a danger to somebody right then, the school can remove you first and do the rest as soon as it can afterward. That is meant for real danger, not for convenience. If you were sent home first, the question to ask later is when the school plans to do the part it skipped.

keyPhrase.quote: When do I get to tell my side of it?
keyPhrase.gloss: Removing you first is the exception, not the order.

scenario.setup: The school office at 8:15, with your bag still on your shoulder.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: You need to go home. We will sort it out later.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: When do I get to tell my side?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Somebody will call you.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. Can my mom get that in writing?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The skipped part becomes something somebody owes you instead of something forgotten.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The order gets reversed and nobody comes back for the missing half.

scenario.note: Go when you are told to go. The question about the missing half is for later, in writing.

questions.q: You are being told you are suspended. What should you ask for before you leave the office?

options.text: The reason, the number of days, and both of those in writing.
Another chance, since asking right away is when that works.
options.explanation: The person telling you often does not decide it, and asking trades away the questions that help.

options.text: A call to your parent, and nothing else for now.
options.explanation: Ask for the call and the paper. A parent with nothing written down is starting from your memory.

options.text: A lawyer, since nothing should happen without one.
options.explanation: A suspension is not a court case. A parent and a piece of paper do more here than a lawyer does.

questions.hint: What will still be useful in a week?
questions.principle: This is the cheapest moment to get three things: what they say you did, how many days, and both of those in writing. Written is what a parent can act on, what an appeal points at, and what keeps the story from changing later. You do not have to argue any of it. Asking is not arguing, and a request for paper is hard for anybody to refuse.

keyPhrase.quote: Can I get the reason and the days in writing?
keyPhrase.gloss: Paper is the part you can use later.

scenario.setup: The doorway of the school office on the way out.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Somebody will call your mom.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can I get the reason and the days in writing?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It'll be in the letter.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. Can I have a copy before I go?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You leave with something a parent can read tonight instead of a memory of a hallway.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The only version of what happened is the one in somebody else's file.

scenario.note: Ask, do not argue. If the answer is no, write down who you asked and when.

questions.q: Who actually decides how long you are out of school?

options.text: The school board, or whoever the board has handed that job to.
The teacher who sent you out, since that is where it started.
options.explanation: A teacher can pull you out of one class for up to a day. How long you are out of school is a different call.

options.text: The board for a suspension, and a principal for an expulsion.
options.explanation: It runs the other way. The longer the removal, the higher up the decision sits.

options.text: A judge, once the number of days gets high enough.
options.explanation: No judge is involved in school discipline. It stays inside the school system.

questions.hint: Does the same person handle one day and sixty?
questions.principle: The authority belongs to the school board. The board can hand it to a superintendent or a principal, and most districts do, which is why a principal is usually the one telling you. An expulsion is the biggest version and normally stays with the board. A teacher has a smaller power. A teacher can pull you out of that one class for up to a full school day, then has to send you to the principal. Ask who is deciding, and who you would ask next.

keyPhrase.quote: Who is making this decision?
keyPhrase.gloss: It is the board's power, handed down as far as the district chooses.

scenario.setup: The hallway outside the school office, waiting to be called in.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Who decides how long it is?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: The principal, for something this length.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: And if it were longer?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Then it goes to the board.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know who to ask and who to ask next, before you need either.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Everybody in the building looks like the person who decided it.

scenario.note: Asking who decides is a normal question. It is not a challenge and nobody minds it.

questions.q: The suspension seems wrong to you. What actually starts a review of it?

options.text: Somebody asking, in writing, before the deadline. A parent usually files it.
Nothing. It gets reviewed on its own if it was wrong.
options.explanation: Nothing reviews itself. A decision nobody challenges just stands.

options.text: A lawyer, since a review is a court thing.
options.explanation: The first review happens inside the school. A parent can start it without a lawyer.

options.text: Only you, and only in person on the day.
options.explanation: A parent or guardian can file it, and it is usually in writing rather than in person.

questions.hint: Who has to move first for anything to happen?
questions.principle: Nothing in school discipline reviews itself. A decision nobody challenges just stands. Who can ask matters. A parent or guardian usually files it, and an adult student can file for themselves. Where it goes is set by your district, and it is often the superintendent or the school board. Ask two things while it is fresh. What the appeal is called here, and when it is due.

keyPhrase.quote: What is the appeal, and when is it due?
keyPhrase.gloss: Somebody has to ask, or it just stands.

scenario.setup: Your kitchen table with the letter between you and your mom.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Do we just take this?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: There's an appeal. I asked what it's called.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Is there a date on it?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Five school days. I wrote it down.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Somebody moves before the deadline, which is the only thing that starts anything.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The date passes and the decision becomes the final version by default.

scenario.note: Get the deadline the same day you get the decision. Deadlines here are short.

questions.q: The suspension is over and you are back. What follows you afterward?

options.text: A school record, not a criminal one. Those are two different files.
A criminal record, since the police were told about it.
options.explanation: School discipline is not a conviction. If there is a police matter, it is a separate record.

options.text: Nothing at all. The days are served, so it is over.
options.explanation: The days ending does not empty the file. Something is written down and it stays written down.

options.text: Everything forever, since schools never take anything off.
options.explanation: Not everything is permanent, and what is depends on what happened. It is a fair question to ask.

questions.hint: Two offices, two folders, two sets of rules.
questions.principle: School discipline lives in your school file. A police case, if there ever is one, is a separate record with its own rules, and a suspension is not a conviction. Some things are permanent by law. An expulsion for certain weapon offenses goes on the permanent record. Most of it is smaller than people think. Ask what went in the file, who can see it, and what comes off later.

keyPhrase.quote: What went in my file, and who sees it?
keyPhrase.gloss: A school file is not a criminal record.

scenario.setup: The school office on the morning you come back.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: What went in my file about this?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: The suspension and the reason.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Who sees that?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Depends who asks.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You find out what exists while you can still ask about it calmly.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You learn what is in the file the first time it matters to somebody else.

scenario.note: Ask on a normal day. Nobody minds the question when nothing is happening.

questions.q: Staff say you agreed to the suspension rules when you signed the handbook in September. Is that right?

options.text: Only partly. A handbook cannot hand the school more than the law allows.
Yes. Signing it is what makes the rules apply to you.
options.explanation: School rules apply whether or not you signed. The signature is a receipt, not the source.

options.text: No. A handbook is a suggestion and nothing more than that.
options.explanation: It is more than a suggestion. It sets out what your district will do, and that is worth reading.

options.text: Yes, and it is why the seven factors do not apply here.
options.explanation: Nothing anybody signs takes the seven factors away. Those come from state law.

questions.hint: Can a piece of paper hand out powers the law did not?
questions.principle: A handbook matters, and it has a ceiling. It tells you what your district plans to do, which you cannot get anywhere else. What it cannot do is hand the school powers the law did not. It also cannot take away what the law requires: the seven factors, the notice, the chance to answer. Signing is not what makes school rules apply. It is still worth reading. A district can promise more than the law asks, and then it has to keep that promise.

keyPhrase.quote: The handbook can add rules. It cannot remove the law.
keyPhrase.gloss: It fills in the district's part, not the state's.

scenario.setup: The school office with a signature page pulled up on a screen.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: You signed this in September.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Does that change what the state law says?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: That's a bigger conversation.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. My mom is going to want to have it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The claim gets tested instead of ending the conversation.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: One signature in September answers everything that happens after it.

scenario.note: You do not have to win this in the room. Get the sentence they said and take it home.

questions.q: Your mom is coming to the school about the suspension. What can she do that you cannot?

options.text: Ask for the file, ask for the written reason, and start the appeal.
Overrule the suspension, since she is your parent.
options.explanation: A parent cannot cancel a school's decision. What she can do is make it get explained and reviewed.

options.text: Very little, since the decision has already been made.
options.explanation: Made is not the same as final. Most of what changes a decision happens after it is made.

options.text: Nothing, since this is between you and the school.
options.explanation: A parent is part of this by design. Records and appeals both run through them, not through you.

questions.hint: What can an adult ask for that a student cannot?
questions.principle: A parent can get things a student usually cannot. Your file. The written reason. A meeting. The appeal. She can also ask whether the seven factors were gone through, which is the question that puts the work back on the school. What she cannot do is cancel the decision. If any of it turns into a police matter, she is not your lawyer, so that part goes to one.

keyPhrase.quote: Ask them whether they went through the seven factors.
keyPhrase.gloss: A parent can ask for things a student cannot.

scenario.setup: The school office with your mom in the chair next to you.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: What do I even ask for?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: The file, the reason in writing, and the appeal.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: And the seven things you told me about?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Ask whether they went through them.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The meeting produces paper, and paper is the thing that can be appealed.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It becomes a conversation about what happened, and nothing leaves the room.

scenario.note: Give a parent the three things to ask for before the meeting, not during it.
